title: One Guru, many sangats
hook: the variety of the panth is its breadth, not its weakness

segments.voice: Yesterday, learning from one stream: a box of virtues opened, and its fragrance shared. Your line was each keeps a treasure. Which practice did you borrow, and how did it go? Day one thousand three hundred sixty.

Someone who listened to this whole block might come away with a worry. Blue-robed Nihangs and white-clad Namdharis. Strict ragas and simple tunes. Meat on one plate, none on another. Arguments over a calendar, a book, the five at the bowl. Isn't a faith with this many streams coming apart at the seams? It's a fair question, and an honest one. Outsiders ask it, and so, sometimes, do Sikhs themselves. Today offers another way to see the same picture.
screen: `SO MANY STREAMS.` → `IS IT COMING APART?` → `ANOTHER WAY TO SEE IT.`

segments.voice: Start with what doesn't vary. The Sikh streams this block visited bow to the same Guru Granth Sahib. The Mool Mantar at its opening names one Creator for all of them. So the sangats are many, and the Guru is one. Now look at the variety again, from the center outward. A banyan tree drops roots from its branches until a single tree looks like a grove. Its width isn't a sign of trouble. It's how the tree holds more shade. The panth has spread across villages and cities, castes and continents, warriors and scholars and singers, and each has taken the same Word into a different life. Gurbani gives the reason the spread doesn't scatter it. In Sohila, the night prayer, Guru Nanak says on Ang 13, here in paraphrase: the one light is in everyone, and that light is the One; by its shining, everyone is lit. If the same light is in each sangat, then many sangats is simply the light, showing up in many rooms. That doesn't make every disagreement easy. This block has been honest that some are hard. But breadth means a Sikh who struggles in one sangat can find another under the same Guru. It means a newcomer in Texas and an elder in Amritsar can open the same page. It means the panth can carry music and martial art, study and service, quiet and loud, without needing them all in one person. The variety is breadth, not weakness.
screen: `ONE GURU, ONE OPENING LINE.` · `A BANYAN WIDENS TO HOLD MORE SHADE.` · `ONE LIGHT IN EVERYONE.` · `MANY ROOMS, THE SAME PAGE.` · then, large: `BREADTH, NOT WEAKNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank the variety. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the streams you've met: the warriors, the scholars, the singers, the quiet ones in white, the newcomers explaining things in English. With each breath, let one of them come forward, and simply say thank you for what they keep. Then widen it to your own life: the people unlike you who make your world bigger. If you pray, you can thank Waheguru for the one light in all of them. The bell holds the time.
One Guru. The Guru Granth Sahib at the center of many sangats: one light, showing up in many rooms. Today's word.
Your line: breadth, not weakness. Today, when a group you love looks divided, name one way its differences make it wider rather than weaker. Day one thousand three hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Sikhs of many streams gather in their own sangats around the same Guru Granth Sahib, and Sohila, the night prayer with its line on the one light in everyone, is recited before sleep.

notes: Ang 13 'sabh meh jot jot hai soi, tis dai chaanan sabh meh chaanan hoi' paraphrased as 'the one light is in everyone, and that light is the One; by its shining, everyone is lit'. Please confirm.
The banyan image is the writer's illustration, not a Gurbani image; Keeper may prefer a Gurbani image.
'A newcomer in Texas and an elder in Amritsar' is illustrative, not a claim about particular sangats.
Word is 'One Guru' (title head, per the outline); the title 'One Guru, many sangats' is kept.

Editor: 'every stream this block visited bows to the same Granth' narrowed to the Sikh streams, since the block's Ravidassia day (1324) notes a separate scripture; same softening in the myth reveal and howItsDone.
